SUBSECT. 15.

Love of Learning, or overmuch study. With a Digression of the misery of Scholars, and why the Muses are Melancholy.

Leonartus Fuchsius Instit. lib. 3 sect. 1 cap. 1§, Felix Plater. lib. 3 de mentis alienat.§, Herc. de Saxonia Tract. post. de melanch. cap. 3, speak of a °° note Peculiaris furor, qui ex literis fit. dmAuthor trans. “peculiar Fury, which comes by overmuch study” peculiar Fury, which comes by overmuch study. For (as Machiavel holds) Study weakens their bodies, dulls the spirits, abates their strength and courage; and good Scholars are never good Soldiers, which a certain Goth well perceived, for when his Countrymen came into Greece, and would have burned all their books, he cried out against it, by all means they should not do it, cc note Gaspar EnsCaspar Ens Thesaur Polit. Hist.Richard Knolles, The Generall Historie of the Turkes .Turks abdicated Corcutus the next heir, from the Empire, because he was so much given to his book: and ’tis the common Tenet of the world, that Learning dulls and diminisheth the spirits, and so per con­se­quensTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.by consequence,djconsequently A scholastic phrase. produceth melancholy.

Two main reasons may be given of it, why Students should be more subject to this malady than others. The one is, they live a sedentary, solitary life, sibi & musisTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.for themselves and the Musesgto themselves and letters,djfor themselves and the Muses A proverbial phrase for a retired life of study. [for themselves and the Muses], free from bodily exercise, and those ordinary disports which other men use: and many times if discontent and idleness concur with it, which is too frequent, they are precipitated into this gulf on a sudden: but the common cause is overmuch study; too much learning (as ee cites Act. 26. 24.Festus told Paul) hath made thee mad; ’tis that other extreme which effects it. So did Trincavellius, lib. 1 consil. 12 & 13§, find by his experience, in two of his Patients, a young Baron, and another that contracted this malady by too vehement study. So Forestus observat. lib. 10 observ. 13, in a young Divine in Louvain§, that was mad, and said °° note Nimiis studiis melancholicus evasit, dicens se Biblium in capite habere. dmAuthor trans. “he had a Bible in his head” He became melancholic through too much study, saying that he had a Bible in his head: Marsilius Ficinus de sanit. tuend. lib. 1 cap. 1, 3, 4§, & lib. 2 cap. 16, gives many reasons, °° note Cur melancholia assidua, crebrisque deliramentis vexentur eorum animi ut desipere cogantur. dmAuthor trans. “why Students dote more often than others” why their minds are troubled with constant melancholy and frequent ravings, so that they are driven out of their wits why Students dote more often than others: the first is their negligence: °° note Solers quilibet artifex instrumenta sua diligentissime curat, penicellos pictor; If you never stop drawing the bow, it will become slackgYou must not imitate the bow and arms of Diana. If you never stop bending it, it will grow slack. Burton cites: Ovid, Heroides (unverified)From Ovid, Heroides 4.91–92 (Phaedra to Hippolytus). As I recall the standard text, it reads 'arcus (et arma tuae tibi sunt imitanda Dianae) / si numquam cesses tendere, mollis erit': you should copy your Diana, who unstrings her bow. Yea, but methinks I hear some man except at these words, that though this be true which I have said of the estate of Scholars, and especially of Divines, that it is miserable and distressed at this time, that the Church suffers shipwreck of her goods, and that they have just cause to complain; there is a fault, but whence proceeds it? If the cause were justly examined, it would be retorted upon ourselves, if we were cited at that Tribunal of truth, we should be found guilty, and not able to excuse it. That there is a fault among us, I confess, and were there not a buyer, there would not be a seller: but to him that will consider better of it, it will more than manifestly appear, that the fountain of these miseries proceeds from these griping Patrons. In accusing them, I do not altogether excuse us; both are faulty, they and we: yet in my judgement, theirs is the greater fault, more apparent causes & much to be condemned. For my part, if it be not with me as I would, or as it should, I do ascribe the cause, as bb cites Lib. 3 de cons.Girolamo Cardano, De consolatione, book 3.Cardan did in the like case, ⁂meo in­for­tu­nio po­tius quam il­lo­rum sce­leriTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Burton translates: “to mine own infelicity, rather than their naughtiness”Burton’s own rendering to my own misfortune rather than to their wickedness , to cc note I had no money, I wanted impudence, I could not scamble, temporize, dissemble: non pran­de­ret olus, &c. I’m a complete fool when it comes to flattering and fawning, I can’t be corrected; I’m too old now to live that way, and don’t want to become like that, even if it turns out badly for me and I skulk in obscurityghe would not dine on greens, etc. Shall I tell you? They toil and moil, but what reap they? They are commonly unfortunate families that use it, accursed in their progeny, & as common experience evinceth, accursed themselves in all their proceedings. A base profane Epicurean, Hypocritical rout; for my part, let them pretend what zeal they will, counterfeit Religion, blear the world’s eyes, bombast themselves, and stuff out their greatness with Church spoils, shine like so many Peacocks; so cold is my charity, so defective in this behalf, that I shall never think better of them, than that they are rotten at core, their bones are full of Epicurean hypocrisy, and Atheistical marrow, they are worse than Heathens. Who reads history, which is like the soul of public conduct? Parents are too hasty in their ambitions, etc.], ’twas Lipsius’ complaint to his illiterate countrymen, it may be ours. Now shall these men judge of a Scholar’s worth, that have no worth, that know not what belongs to a student’s labours, that cannot distinguish between a true scholar and a drone? Or him that by reason of a voluble tongue, a strong voice, a pleasing tone, and some trivantly Polyanthean helps, steals and gleans a few notes from other men’s Harvests, and so makes a fairer show, than him that is truly learned indeed: that thinks it no more to preach, than to speak, vv note Dr. King, in his last lecture on Jonah, sometimes right reverend Lord Bishop of London.John King, Lectures upon Jonas, last lecture .or to run away with an empty Cart; as a grave man said; and thereupon vilify us, and our pains; scorn us, and all learning. ww note Qui­bus opes & otium, hi bar­baro fastu li­te­ras con­tem­nuntTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Wealthy and leisured, these people disdain letters with barbarous arrogancegThose who have wealth and leisure despise letters with barbarous arrogance [Wealthy and leisured, these people disdain letters with barbarous arrogance].Wealthy and leisured, these people disdain letters with barbarous arrogance gBecause they are rich, and have other means to live, they think it concerns them not to know, or to trouble themselves with it; a fitter task for younger brothers, or poor men’s sons, to be pen and Ink-horn men, pedantical slaves, and no whit beseeming the calling of a Gentleman, as Frenchmen and Germans commonly do, neglect therefore all humane learning, what have they to do with it? Let Mariners learn Astronomy; Merchants’ Factors study Arithmetic; Surveyors get them Geometry; Spectacle-makers Optics; Land-leapers Geography; Town Clerks Rhetoric, what should he do with a spade, that hath no ground to dig; or they with Learning, that have no use of it? Thus they reason, and are not ashamed to let Mariners, Prentices, and the basest servants be better qualified than themselves. In former times, Kings, Princes, and Emperors were the only Scholars, excellent in all faculties. Julius Caesar mended the year, and writ his own Commentaries,

The line means that learning is its own reward, since it brings the scholar no other. [Knowledge itself is a dowry, and a bounty for itself].Well done, good gKnowledge itself is a dowry, and a bounty for itself ga proper man, and ’tis pity he hath no preferment, all good wishes, but inexorable, indurate as he is, he will not prefer him, though it be in his power, because he is ⁂in­do­ta­tusTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Burton translates: “he hath no money”Burton’s own rendering undowered , he hath no money. Or if he do give him entertainment, let him be never so well qualified, plead affinity, consanguinity, sufficiency, he shall serve seven years, as Jacob did for Rachel, before he shall have it. ww note Qua­tuor ad por­tas Ec­cle­sias itur ad omnes; san­gui­nis aut Si­mo­nis, prae­su­lis atque DeiTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.The four doors for entering into all churches: birth, simony, patronage and GodgThere are four gates by which one comes to every church: that of blood, or of Simon, of the prelate, and of God Burton cites: Robert Holcot (unverified)'Ecclesias' appears to stand for 'Ecclesiae' or 'ecclesias … omnes' ('to all churches'). The four gates are kinship, simony (from Simon Magus), a bishop's favour, and merit or a true calling. Burton's 'Simoniacal gate' in the main text picks up only the second of these. [The four doors for entering into all churches: birth, simony, patronage and God]. Holcot.Robert Holcot.The four doors for entering into all churches: birth, simony, patronage and God gIf he will enter at first, he must get in at that Simoniacal gate, come off soundly, and put in good security to perform all covenants, else he will not deal with, or admit him. But if some poor scholar, some parson chuff, will offer himself; some Trencher Chaplain, that will take it to the halves, thirds, or accept of what he will give, he is welcome; be conformable, preach as he will have him, he likes him before a million of others; for the best is always best cheap: and then as Jerome said to Cromatius, pa­tella di­gnum oper­cu­lumTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.the lid’s fitting for the dishg'Tis a cover worthy of the potdja lid worthy of the dish Burton cites: Jerome, Letter to Chromatius (unverified)A proverb, like the English 'like pot, like lid'. Burton applies it in his own words rather than translating it. [the lid’s fitting for the dish], such a Patron, such a Clerk; the cure is well supplied, and all parties pleased. So that is still verified in our age, which xx cites Lib. contra Gentiles de Babila martyre.John Chrysostom, De sancto Babyla, contra Julianum et gentiles .Chrysostom complained of in his time, ⁂Qui opu­len­tio­res sunt, in or­di­nem pa­ra­si­to­rum co­gunt eos, & ipsos tan­quam canes ad men­sas suas enu­triunt, eo­rum­que im­pu­den­tes Ven­tres ini­qua­rum coe­na­rum re­li­quiis dif­fer­tiunt, iis­dem pro ar­bi­trio abu­ten­tesTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Burton translates: “rich men keep these Lecturers, and fawning Parasites, like so many dogs at their tables, and filling their hungry guts with the offals of their meat, they abuse them at their pleasure, and make them say what they propose”Burton’s own rendering The wealthier sort force them into the ranks of parasites, rear them like dogs at their tables, stuff their shameless bellies with the leavings of their wicked dinners, and abuse them as they please : rich men keep these Lecturers, and fawning Parasites, like so many dogs at their tables, and filling their hungry guts with the offals of their meat, they abuse them at their pleasure, and make them say what they propose. yy cites Heinsius.Daniel Heinsius.As children do by a bird or a butterfly in a string, pull in and let him out as they list, do they by their trencher Chaplains, prescribe, command their wits, let in and out as to them it seems best. If the Patron be precise, so must his Chaplain be, if he be papistical, his Clerk must be so too, or else be turned out. These are those Clerks which serve the turn, whom they commonly entertain, and present to Church livings, whilst in the meantime we that are University men, like so many hidebound Calves in a Pasture, tarry out our time, wither away as a flower ungathered in a garden, & are never used: or as so many candles, illuminate ourselves alone, obscuring one another’s light, & are not discerned here at all, the least of which, translated to a dark room, or to some Country benefice, where it might shine apart, would give a fair light, and be seen over all. Whilst we lie waiting here as those sick men did at the pool of zz cites Joh. 5.John 5.Bethesda, till the Angel stirred the water, expecting a good hour, they step between, and beguile us of our preferment. I have not yet said, if after long expectation, much expense, travel, earnest suit of ourselves and friends, we obtain a small Benefice at last: our misery begins afresh, we are suddenly encountered with the flesh, world, and Devil, with a new onset; we change a quiet life for an ocean of troubles, we come to a ruinous house, which before it be habitable, must be necessarily to our great damage repaired; we are compelled to sue for dilapidations, or else sued ourselves, and, scarce yet settled, we are called upon for our Predecessor’s arrearages; first fruits, tenths, subsidies, are instantly to be paid, benevolence, procurations, &c., and which is most to be feared, we light upon a cracked title, as it befell Clenard of Brabant, for his rectory and charge of his Be­gi­naeTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Beguines The Beguines were lay religious communities of women in the Low Countries. Clenard had charge of a Beguine house as part of his benefice.; he was no sooner inducted, but instantly sued, ce­pi­mus­queTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.and we began Burton cites: Nicolaus Clenardus, Letters (unverified)The phrase is cut off by Burton's '(saith he)'. It continues in the next passage: 'strenue litigare …'. (aa cites Epist. lib. 2.Nicolaus Clenardus, Epistolae, book 2 .saith he) strenue li­ti­gare, & im­pla­ca­bili bello con­fli­gereTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.and we started … to litigate vigorously and to fight a relentless wargto go to law vigorously, and to fight it out in implacable war Burton cites: Nicolaus Clenardus, Letters (unverified)This completes 'cepimusque': 'and we began to go to law vigorously …'. [and we started … to litigate vigorously and to fight a relentless war]: at length after ten years’ suit, as long as Troy’s siege, when he had tired himself, and spent his money, he was fain to leave all for quietness’ sake, and give it up to his adversary. Or else we are insulted over, and trampled on by domineering officers, fleeced by those greedy Harpies to get more fees; we stand in fear of some precedent Lapse; we fall amongst refractory, seditious Sectaries, peevish Puritans, perverse Papists, a lascivious rout of Atheistical Epicures, that will not be reformed, or some litigious people (those wild beasts of Ephesus, must be fought with) that will not pay their dues without much repining, or compelled by long suit; for Laici cle­ri­cis op­pido in­fe­stiTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.the laity are thoroughly inimical to the clergygthe generality of laymen despise the clergy,djLaymen are exceedingly hostile to clerics Probably: Boniface VIII, Clericis laicos (papal bull) (unverified)Burton calls this 'an old axiom'. It echoes the opening of Boniface VIII's bull Clericis laicos (1296): 'Clericis laicos infestos oppido tradit antiquitas' ('antiquity teaches that laymen are exceedingly hostile to clerics'). [the laity are thoroughly inimical to the clergy], an old axiom, all they think well-gotten that is had from the Church, and by such uncivil, harsh dealings, they make their poor Minister weary of his place, if not his life: and put case they be quiet honest men, make the best of it, as often it falls out, from a polite and terse Academic, he must turn rustic, rude, melancholize alone, learn to forget, or else, as many do, become Maltsters, Graziers, Chapmen, &c. (now banished from the Academy, all commerce of the Muses, and confined to a country village, as Ovid was from Rome to Pontus), and daily converse with a company of Idiots and Clowns.

(tem­plum est vae­nale, deus­queTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.the temple is for sale, and God too A verse tag set in parentheses inside Burton's Latin. It sounds like a quotation, but no source is given.), tot sor­desTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.so much filth Sordes means moral filth and also sordid, mercenary dealing. in­ve­han­tur, tanta gras­se­tur im­pie­tas, tanta ne­qui­tia, tam in­sa­nus mi­se­ra­rium Eu­ri­pus, & tur­ba­rum ae­stua­rium, no­stro in­quam, om­niumTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.are brought in, such impiety runs riot, such wickedness, so mad a Euripus of miseries and so seething a tide of troubles, by our fault, I say, of all of us The subject 'tot sordes' ('so much filth') comes just before the passage, and '(Academicorum imprimis) vitio fit' ('above all of the academics … it comes about by the fault') comes just after it. 'Miserarium' is evidently a misprint for 'miseriarum' ('of miseries'). The Euripus was the strait at Chalcis, famous for its violent, shifting currents. Sponsi Pe­ne­lo­pes, ne­bu­lo­nes, Al­ci­noi­que,Translation from Latin: from LatinLat.Penelope's suitors, good-for-nothings, and Alcinous' young men, Probably: Horace, Epistles, 1.2.28 (unverified)A line of Horace that Burton works into his own Latin attack on the universities. Horace means idle young men who live only to eat and to look after themselves. Here it describes the poor, unfit scholars who are pushed into the Church.

modo tot annos in Aca­de­mia in­sump­se­rintTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.provided only they have spent so many years at the University , & se pro to­ga­tis ven­di­ta­rintTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.and have passed themselves off as gownsmen togati: men who wear the academic gown, that is, members of the university.; lucriTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.of gain Part of 'lucri causa', 'for the sake of gain'. causa, & ami­co­rum in­ter­cessu prae­sen­tan­turTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.sake, and are presented at the intercession of friends The passage begins in mid-phrase. Acad. cap. 6.' may give the source, but its link to this phrase is uncertain.) id unum cu­rant, ut ex pro­fes­sio­ni­bus fre­quen­ti­bus, & tu­mul­tua­riis po­tius quam le­gi­ti­mis, com­moda sua pro­mo­veant, & ex di­spen­dio pu­blico suum fa­ciant in­cre­men­tumTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.care for this one thing only: that by frequent conferrings of degrees, hurried rather than lawful, they may advance their own profit, and make their own gain out of the public loss Burton cites: Acad., cap. 6 (unverified)professiones here probably means the conferring of degrees, or admissions to them. tumultuarius: done in haste and irregularly. Id solumTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.This alone Fragment: the opening words of the sentence 'Id solum in votis habent annui plerumque magistratus…' ('This alone is what the annual officers mostly wish for…'). Only the marked words are translated. in votis ha­bent annui ple­rum­que ma­gi­stra­tus, ut ab in­ci­pien­tium nu­meroTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.the yearly officers for the most part make it their prayer that, from the number of inceptors A fragment cut off at both ends. The full sentence reads: 'This alone the yearly officers for the most part wish for: to squeeze money out of the number of inceptors.' 'Annui magistratus' are presumably the annually elected university officers, such as the proctors. 'Incipientes' are 'inceptors', candidates taking their degree. cc note Ac­ci­pia­mus pe­cu­niam, de­mit­ta­mus asi­num ut apud Pa­ta­vi­nos, Ita­losTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Let us take the money and send the ass away, as among the Paduans, Italians A mocking graduation formula, apparently proverbial, said to be used at Padua: take the fee and send the ignorant candidate off with his degree..Let us take the money and send the ass away, as among the Paduans, Italians pecunias emungant, nec multum interest qui sint, literatores an literati, modo pingues, nitidi, ad aspectum speciosi, & quod verbo dicam, pecuniosi sint. dd note Hos non ita pri­dem per­strinxi, inTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.I lashed these men not long ago, in The marked portion stops in mid-sentence. Phi­lo­so­pha­stro Co­moe­dia la­tina, in Aede Chri­sti Oxon. pu­blice ha­bitaTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Philosophaster, a Latin comedy, publicly performed at Christ Church, Oxford Burton refers to his own Latin comedy Philosophaster. And hence The subject, Theologastri (solvant modo), comes just before the passage: 'Divinitasters, provided only they pay'. The final 'Atque hinc' runs on into 'fit quod...': 'and hence it comes about that...'. fitTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.it comes about A single word from 'Atque hinc fit quod…' ('And hence it comes about that…'). quod tam viles scur­rae, tot pas­simTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.that such vile buffoons, so many everywhere The sentence goes on 'Idiotae ...' ('ignoramuses ...'). The passage is a fragment of the longer sentence. Idio­tae, li­te­ra­rum cre­pu­sculo po­siti, lar­vae pa­sto­rum, cir­cum­fo­ra­nei, vagi, bardi, fungi, crassi, asini, merum pecus in sa­cro­sanc­tos theo­lo­giae adi­tus, il­lo­tis pe­di­bus ir­rum­pant, prae­ter in­ve­re­cun­dam fron­tem ad­fe­ren­tes nihil, vul­ga­res qua­sdam qui­squi­lias, & scho­la­rium quae­dam nu­ga­menta, in­di­gna quae vel re­ci­pian­turTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.ignoramuses, standing in the twilight of learning, mere ghosts of pastors, strolling mountebanks, vagabonds, dolts, blockheads, clods, asses, mere cattle, burst with unwashed feet into the sacred precincts of theology, bringing nothing but a shameless brow, some common rubbish and certain schoolboy trifles, unworthy to be received even The sentence ends just outside the marked text with 'in triviis' ('at the crossroads', i.e. in the street). 'Idiotae' means unlearned men; 'larvae pastorum' means masks or spectres of shepherds; 'fungi' (mushrooms) is a stock Latin insult for blockheads. The phrase 'illotis pedibus' (with unwashed feet) is proverbial for irreverent entry into sacred things. in tri­viis. Hoc illud in­di­gnum genus ho­mi­num & fa­me­li­cum, in­di­gnum, vagum, ven­tris man­ci­pium, ad sti­vam po­tius re­le­gan­dum, ad haras ap­tius quam ad aras, quod di­vi­nas hasce li­te­ras tur­pi­ter pro­sti­tuitTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.at the street-corners. This is that unworthy and famished race of men, unworthy, vagrant, slaves of the belly, who ought rather to be sent back to the plough-handle, fitter for the sties than for the shrines, who basely prostitute these divine letters 'In triviis' ends the previous sentence ('trifles unworthy to be received even at the street-corners'). 'Ad haras aptius quam ad aras' is a jingle: 'haras' means pigsties and 'aras' means altars. 'Sties … shrines' keeps some of the alliteration.; hi sunt qui pul­pita com­plentTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.these are they who fill the pulpits , in aedes no­bi­lium ir­re­punt, & quum re­li­quis vitae de­sti­tuan­tur sub­si­diis, ob cor­po­ris & animi ege­sta­tem, alia­rumTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.they creep into noblemen's houses, and since they are destitute of other means of living, and through poverty of body and mind are of other The fragment breaks off at 'aliarum', which goes with the words that follow outside the marked text: 'are hardly capable of any other functions in the commonwealth'. The partial phrase at the end is translated as it stands. ff cites 2 Cor. 2. 17.2 Corinthians 2:17.For we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ. kjvin Repub. par­tium mi­nime ca­pa­ces sint; ad sa­cram hanc an­cho­ram con­fu­giunt, sa­cer­do­tium quo­vi­smodo cap­tan­tes, non ex sin­ce­ri­tate, quod Pau­lus aitTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.in the commonwealth, are scarcely capable of filling; they flee to this sacred anchor, catching at a priesthood by any means whatever, not out of sincerity, as Paul says Burton cites: Paul, 2 Corinthians, 2. 17 (unverified)'aliarum' (other), which governs 'partium', stands just before the marked text: they are scarcely capable of any other roles in the commonwealth. The Pauline phrase continues outside the marked text with 'sed cauponantes verbum Dei' ('but huckstering the word of God')., sed cau­po­nan­tes ver­bum DeiTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.but peddling the word of God Burton cites: Paul, 2 Corinthians, 2. 17 (unverified)cauponantes means 'dealing like tavern-keepers or hucksters' and renders the Greek of 2 Corinthians 2:17. The Vulgate has 'adulterantes' instead.. Ne quis in­te­rim viris bonis de­trac­tum quid putet, quos habetTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Meanwhile let no one think that anything is taken away from the good men, whom it has The subject of 'habet' comes after the passage: 'Ecclesia Anglicana quamplurimos', 'whom the English Church has in great numbers'. The 'following English' suggested as a candidate is in fact Latin. Ec­cle­sia An­gli­cana quam­plu­ri­mos, egre­gie doc­tos, il­lu­stresTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.the Church of England has very many, excellently learned, illustrious Fragment of 'quos habet Ecclesia Anglicana quamplurimos…', in which Burton says the Church of England has a great many good men, excellently learned, illustrious, of spotless reputation. 'habet' stands before the marked text., in­tac­tae famae ho­mi­nes, & plu­res for­san quam quae­vis Eu­ro­pae pro­vin­ciaTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.men of untouched reputation, and more perhaps than any province of Europe This continues the list of the good men of the English Church. The 'preceding English' suggested as a candidate is in fact Latin.; ne quis a flo­ren­tis­si­misTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.nor let anyone think anything detracted from the most flourishing The construction is elliptical. It repeats 'Ne quis … detractum quid putet' from earlier in the sentence, so 'think anything detracted' is supplied from there. The noun 'Academiis' (universities) follows just outside the marked text. Aca­de­miis, quae viros un­di­qua­que doc­tis­si­mos, omni vir­tu­tum ge­nere su­spi­cien­dos, abunde pro­du­cunt. Et multo plu­res utra­que ha­bi­tura, multo splen­di­dior fu­tura, si non haeTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.universities, which abundantly produce men most learned in every respect and worthy of admiration for every kind of virtue. [Meanwhile, as far as we’re concerned (for we’re not free of this fault), the same charge remains, and the same accusation, if not a much more serious one, can be levelled at us: for it’s due to our guilt, our negligence, our greed, that there are such frequent and abominable traffickings in the Church (‘the temple is for sale, and the god’), that so much squalor is brought into it, that there’s such great impiety around, such wickedness, such an insane tide of miseries and marsh of troubles, I say it is our fault, and especially that of academics. All the evils afflicting the commonwealth are from our nursery; we summoned this mischief ourselves, and deserve every reproach, every misery, for not vigorously resisting it. What else could we hope for, when every day and without discrimination, poor locals, lowly good-for-nothings, and petty men of all ranks are eagerly admitted for degrees? People who, if they have memorized one or two definitions and distinctions, and invested the customary number of years in logic, no matter what progress they’ve made, or that they finally turn out to be idiots, jokers, idlers, gamers, drunkards, reprobates, servants of lust and pleasure,

The suitors of Penelope, the idle rascals of Alcinous,

just so long as they have spent so many years in the University, and boasted about wearing gowns, they are given degrees because of their wealth and the intercession of friends; I add that they’re also often honoured with glorious eulogies of their character and knowledge in gushing testimonials written for them by those who undoubtedly jettison their honesty and reputation. ‘For doctors and professors’ (as {Franciscus Junius the Elder} says) ‘care only for this one thing, that in their numerous occupations, which are more irregular than legitimate, they can increase their profit and make their own gain at public expense.’ Most of the annual office-holders have only one wish: to cheat those graduating out of their qq note Let’s take the money and dismiss the dolt, as the Paduans do in Italy.money, without much regard for who they are, elementary teachers or scholars, only that they are plump, sleek, handsome in appearance, and, in a word, rich. rr note I censured these people not long ago in Philosophaster, a Latin comedy, presented at Christ Church, Oxford, on 16 February 1617.Philosophasters who have no art are made Masters of Arts, ‘And people are decreed to be wise, who possess no wisdom, and contribute nothing to their degree besides the wish for it.’ Theologasters who are sufficiently and exceedingly learned (so long as they pay) are elevated and ascend through all the ranks of honours. And hence it is that such worthless buffoons, so many idiots everywhere, standing in the twilight of learning, masqueraders of pastors, itinerants, vagrants, dolts, dunces, dullards, blockheads and mere cattle gain access to the sacrosanct domains of theology, bursting in with dirty feet, bringing nothing but a shameless face, some commonplace rubbish and some scholarly trifles, which aren’t even fit to be heard on the street. This is that unworthy and famished class of men, destitute, vagrant, slaves of their bellies, which should be banished to the plough handle, more suited to pigsties than altars, which filthily prostitutes our divine learning; these are the men who fill the pulpits, steal into noble houses, and since they are deprived of any other means of living by their mental and bodily deficiency, are barely capable of doing anything else in the commonwealth; they flee to this sacred refuge, seizing on to the priesthood by any means they can, not out of integrity, as Paul says, ‘but trafficking in the word of God’. Meanwhile, let no one think that this is any disparagement of the many good men that the Church of England contains, outstandingly learned, illustrious men of spotless integrity, and more numerous perhaps than in any province of Europe; nor of the most flourishing universities, which produce in abundance men who are most knowledgeable in every branch of learning, and to be recognized for every kind of virtue. And both universities would have many more, and would be far more distinguished, if these dregs did not darken their brilliant light, if corruption did not stand in the way, and haggling harpies and lowly men did not envy our excellence. For no one has a mind so blind that they don’t see this themselves, no one’s so dull-witted that they don’t understand, of such stubborn judgement that they don’t recognize that sacred theology has been polluted by these vile fools, and that they have prostituted the heavenly Muses as if they were something profane. ‘Base and insolent souls’ (as indeed Luther calls them somewhere), ‘for the sake of a small profit, they scurry to the tables of nobles and illustrious men, like flies to a milk-pail, in the hope of a benefice’, and rush into any court or city, prepared for any occupation.

He is led around … like a wooden puppet by another’s wires …

following the morsel, like parrots, they babble out whatever you want in the hope of gain: ‘Obsequious Parasites’ (Erasmus says), ‘they teach, say, write, advise and approve anything you want against their conscience, not for the salvation of their flock, but to contrive their own splendid fortune. They assert any opinions and principles against the word of God, in order not to offend their patron, to retain the favour of the great and the applause of the people, and to amass riches for themselves.’ Indeed, very many of them turn their minds to theology not as a divine matter, but for their own purpose; not to advance the good of the Church, but to pillage it; seeking, as Paul says, ‘not the things of Jesus Christ, but their own things’, they gather not the treasure of the lord, but treasure for themselves and their families. Nor is this only the practice of those of meaner fortune and humbler rank: this evil has seized the middle and upper classes, exalted men, not to say bishops.

Tell us, pontiffs, what’s gold doing amongst sacred things?

‘Greed often leads the most eminent men astray’, and those who outshine others with their upright character; they lead the way to simony, and dashing against this rock of corruption, not only shear the flock but flay it, and wherever they go, they pillage, drain, extort, making a shipwreck of their reputation, if not their souls: so the evil seems to have spread not from the bottom to the top, but from the top to the bottom, and that which someone once joked is true, ‘What he first bought, he can rightly sell.’ ‘For the simoniac’ (I say this with Leo) ‘hasn’t received a favour, and if he doesn’t receive it, he doesn’t have it, and if he doesn’t have it, he can’t be grateful’; in fact, some of those who sit at the helm are so far from promoting others that they thoroughly obstruct them, being very well aware of the skills by which they attained their own position. ‘For he who believes that he has risen because of his learning is a fool: he who thinks that it’s the reward for actual genius, erudition, experience, honesty, piety, and devotion to the Muses’ (which once was true, and today is only expected) ‘is most clearly insane.’ However or from wherever this evil originated, I shall not further enquire; from these beginnings arose the foulest vices, every calamity, all the multitude of miseries that assail the Church. Hence such frequent simony, hence the complaints that have arisen, the deceits, the impostures; every wickedness derives from this source. I shall not speak, by the way, of ambition, of flattery greater than in courts (in order that they don’t suffer a dismal dinner at home), of luxury, of the sometimes loathsome example of their life, by which they offend a good many, of their sybaritic drinking, etc. Hence that academic squalor, ‘the sorrow of the Muses in these times’, when any petty man ignorant of the arts can rise by these skills, be promoted and grow rich in this way, be distinguished with ostentatious titles, be venerable with many dignities and dazzle the eyes of the masses, and revel in it, strutting around loftily and exhibiting a certain grandeur and extraordinary punctiliousness, with a venerable beard, an elegant gown, gleaming in purple, and attracting the most attention for his magnificent household and numerous servants. ‘Like the statues’ (as {Budaeus} says) ‘placed on columns in sacred buildings, which look as if they are giving way under their load, and sweating, when in truth they have no feeling, and add nothing to the strength of the stone’, they want to seem Atlases, when they are actually stony statues, shadowy little men, dolts perhaps and dullards, no different from rock. Meanwhile, men who are learned and endowed with the graces of a more holy life, who endure the heat of the day, by unjust fate serve these men; content perhaps with a tiny salary, addressed with simple titles, humble, obscure – although much more worthy – destitute and unrewarded, they lead their own private lives, entombed in poor parishes, or incarcerated forever in their colleges, and lie hidden without fame. But I don’t want to stir up this filthy water any more; hence these tears, the Muses being in mourning, hence religion itself (as I say with Sesellius) ‘is led into ridicule and contempt’, the priesthood degraded; and this being so, I dare to say (borrowing the rotten saying of a rotten fellow about the clergy) they are ‘a rotten mob’: mean, coarse, squalid, melancholy, miserable, despicable, contemptible.]

moreSource Probably Horace, Epistles, 1.2.28 (unverified)

The verb 'faciunt' ('make, incur') falls outside the marked text, so the gap is shown with an ellipsis.

Not to say anything in passing of ambition, of flattery more than courtly so that they need not suffer a sad dinner at home, of luxury, of the sometimes foul example of life by which they give offence to some, of Sybaritic drinking-bouts, etc. Hence that academic squalor

Burton changes the accusative to the nominative. trans. when any manikin ignorant of the arts rises by these arts, is promoted in this way and grows rich, distinguished by ambitious titles and, made august by many dignities, dazzles the eyes of the crowd, lives well, and, stepping grandly, displays a certain majesty and greatness and a wonderful air of solicitude, reverend in beard, sleek in gown, glittering in purple, most conspicuous for the splendour of his furniture and the number of his servants

moreNotes The preceding 'Atlantes' completes the sense: 'they want to seem Atlases', bearing the weight of the Church like Atlas holding up the sky. 'Umbratiles' means living in the shade, idle and insubstantial.
trans. blockheads perhaps and dullards, no different from a stone. Meanwhile learned men, endowed with the ornaments of a holier life, who bear the heat of the day, serve these by an unjust lot, content perhaps with the smallest salary, called by their bare names, humble, obscure, and though far worthier, needy and unhonoured, they lead a private, retired life, and buried in some poor benefice, or imprisoned for ever in their colleges, they lie hidden without glory. But I will stir this sink no longer; hence those tears, the mourning habit of the Muses, hence religion itself (as I may say with Seyssel
moreNotes 'Fungi' (mushrooms) is a common Latin insult for dull, senseless people. 'Qui aestum diei sustinent' echoes Matthew 20:12. 'Puris nominibus' means names without titles or degrees. 'Vitam privam privatam' is a doubled jingle; its exact force is uncertain. The passage ends inside Burton's parenthesis, before its closing bracket.
trans. is brought into mockery and contempt
moreSource Burton cites Claude de Seyssel, de rep. Gallorum, Lib. 1 (unverified)Notes The subject is 'ipsa religio', religion itself.
trans. the priesthood made abject trans. and where these things happen, I would dare to say it, and the rank
moreNotes The parenthesis continues 'putidi dicterium de clero usurpare': 'and borrow the rank jibe of a rank man about the clergy'. The repeated putidum/putidi is a deliberate jingle.
trans. to borrow a rotten fellow's gibe about the clergy
moreNotes The word 'putidum' just before the marked words belongs with them: 'putidum putidi dicterium', 'the rotten gibe of a rotten man'. The rotten man is evidently Campion (sidenote 'Campian.'), whose slur follows.
trans. A rotten rabble
moreSource Burton cites Edmund Campion (unverified)Notes This begins the 'rotten man's' jibe about the clergy. The list continues 'inops, rude' ('needy, uncouth').
trans. needy, uncouth
moreSource Burton cites Edmund Campion (unverified)Notes Part of the quoted gibe 'Putidum vulgus, inops, rude, sordidum…' ('a rotten rabble, needy, uncouth, sordid…') against the English clergy.
trans. sordid, melancholy, wretched, despicable, contemptible
moreSource Burton cites Edmund Campion (unverified)Notes These words end Campion's jibe about the clergy.
cites Leonhart Fuchs (Fuchsius), book 3, section 1, chapter 1cites Felix Platter (Platerus), De mentis alienatione, book 3cites Jean Fernel, book 1, chapter 18cites Giovanni Arcolani (Arculanus), book 9cites Rhazes, Liber ad Almansorem, chapter 16cites Levinus Lemnius, De occultis naturae miraculis, book 1, chapter 16 cites Marsilio Ficino (Ficinus), book 1, chapter 7cites Vettore Trincavelli (Trincavellius), book 1, consilium 12, 13cites Pieter van Foreest (Forestus), book 10, observation 13cites Marsilio Ficino (Ficinus), book 1, chapter 1, 3, 4cites Bernardino Gómez Miedes (Gomesius), book 4, chapter 1cites probably Gregor Nymann, Oratio de imaginatione; Jo. Voschius, De peste, book 2, chapter 5 cites Seneca, Epistulae morales, letter 8 cites Franz Hildesheim, Spicilegium, book 2, De mania et delirio cites Vettore Trincavelli (Trincavellius), book 3, consilium 36, consilium 17cites Giovanni Battista da Monte (Montanus), consilium 233cites Girolamo Mercuriale, consilium 86, consilium 25cites Prosper Calanius, De atra bile cites Battista Fregoso (Fulgosus), De dictis factisque memorabilibus, book 8, chapter 7 cites Michael Marullus, book 2, chapter 4cites Alessandro Alessandri, Genialium dierum libri, book 6, chapter 16 cites Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Antiquitates Romanae, book 7 gloss belike It is likely or probably; perhaps w gloss informed Instructed, taught gloss informed Instructed, educated gloss compassed Obtained, procured gloss Maul Implacable foe, scourge.gloss institution Education or instruction.about Corcutus Prince Korkut (1467–1513), the son of Sultan Bayezid II.gloss Pencils Brushes.gloss President Presiding deity or guardian.see Crudities, Oppilations See above, .about great Tostatus’ … Works A reference to the influential Spanish theologian and Hebraic scholar Alfonso Tostado Ribera de Madrigal (c. 1400–1455), also known as ‘Abulensis’ after becoming bishop of Avila in 1449.note the other on his Almagest That is, Ptolemy on his famous astronomical and mathematical treatise, known as the Almagest after the Arabic version that was translated into Latin in the twelfth century.about to find out the motion of the eighth sphere The treatise De motu octave sphere was commonly attributed, possibly falsely, to the Mesopotamian mathematician and astronomer Thabit ibn Qurra (c. 830–901). The eighth cosmological ‘sphere’ in question was traditionally held to contain the fixed stars, located beyond the preceding seven spheres (which contained the planets): see above, .gloss Clown A rustic, or peasant.gloss make congees Take ceremonious leave.gloss Swasher Ostentatious braggart or swaggerer.source They cannot fiddle … great City Note ‘b’ relates an anecdote given by Plutarch about Themistocles when taunted about his lack of cultured sophistication, contrasting his inability to play the lyre or harp with his civic achievements (Themistocles 2.3).about King Lewis of France Louis IX, who reigned 1226–70.about conclusum est contra Manichaeos In the Summa theologiae (1266–73), Thomas Aquinas criticized the ancient belief-system of Manicheanism, which posited a primeval cosmological conflict between the forces of Good and Evil, as an especially grievous form of superstitious idolatry because of its exaltation of two opposed gods. In the thirteenth century, the ascetic heretical sect of the Cathars in southern France were sometimes regarded as Manichean revivalists.note notice of it These famous anecdotes about Archimedes arise from his friendship with Hieron II of Syracuse (ruled c. 271–216 BCE), whom he had helped with improvements to the city’s defences. The mathematician was killed by a Roman soldier when the city was sacked after the long siege of 213–212 BCE, because he refused to stop contemplating a geometrical diagram.about where he was This story about Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153) refers to his journeying around Lake Geneva (named ‘Lacus Lemannus’ by the Romans) in the spring of 1137.about Menedemus Lampsacus A Cynic philosopher of the third century BCE, who was a pupil of two philosophers from Lampsacus in western Asia Minor, Colotes the Epicurean and Echecles the Cynic.gloss circumvented Outwitted, cheated.gloss Sots Fools, blockheads.about Paglarensis The eminent fourteenth-century Sienese jurist Giovanni Pagliarese.about Isaeus Isaeus the Assyrian, a rhetorician who was famous in Rome c. 100 CE; see also below, 3.2.5.2.gloss mewed up Confined or caged up – see above, .gloss driven to their shifts Pushed to the last extremity, to the point of extreme difficulty or ‘last resort’.gloss saving Breaking even, or turning a modest profit.gloss docile Teachable.about Kings can invest Knights … confessed Sigismund of Luxembourg (1368–1437) who as Holy Roman Emperor knighted the jurist Georgius Fistellus, but then rebuked him at a session of the Council of Basel (1431–5) for seating himself with the knights rather than the doctors of law. The emperor’s point, reportedly, was that he could make a thousand knights in one day, but not even a single doctor in a thousand years.gloss compass Lay hold of, obtain.gloss parable Procurable.gloss stump rod A teacher’s rod used to punish pupils, worn to a stump by repeated use.note trencher Chaplain A contemptuous term for a domestic chaplain, who eats at the table of a noble patron.about Satyricon In note ‘d’, a reference to the Euphormionis lusinini satyricon (1605–7) by John Barclay (rather than the work of Petronius).note a Living to the halves With a half-share of a benefice.gloss mother of the maids A housekeeper in charge of the maids, but alternatively, a brothel-keeper.note cracked Chambermaid A morally or physically impaired (by implication, deflowered) lady’s maid – although a maid who cleans bedrooms is also possible.note as Hercules did by Cacus Scenes from the life of Heracles (Hercules) in classical mythology: his defeat of the shape-shifting river-god Achelous, a rival suitor for Deianira – on whom, see below, ; his fifth labour, to clean the stables of King Augeas in a single day; his killing of two tyrants, the Thracian king Diomedes, who owned a team of man-eating mares which were kept supplied with human victims (during his eighth labour), and the Egyptian king Busiris, who habitually slaughtered foreigners entering Egypt (during his eleventh labour); his killing of the giant Cacus and the robber Lacinius after they had stolen from him some of the cattle he had been sent to obtain from the giant Geryon (his tenth labour); and his rescue of the Trojan princess Hesione from a sea-monster sent by Poseidon (Neptune).about Mathematicians The astronomer Christoph Rothmann (c. 1560–c. 1600), who served William IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel (1532–92), was not actually a ‘mathematician’ in the obsolete sense of ‘astrologer’ meant here; he has been confused with Johann Rothmann, author of Chiromantiae theorica, practica, concordantia genethliaca (1595).about Sophisters Here, probably, logicians (without the usual pejorative contrast with philosophers).note ranas In classical mythology, at the request of Eos (Aurora), Zeus (Jupiter) granted her lover Tithonus immortality; but when Tithonus became old and helpless, he gradually turned into a cicada. Leto (Latona), the mother of Apollo and Artemis (Diana), arranged for Zeus to turn a group of Lycian peasants into frogs when they refused to let her drink from their pond.gloss viaticum Travel money or supplies.note Manucodiatae those Indian Birds of Paradise … no other food Since birds of paradise were first brought to Europe from the East Indies in the sixteenth century as skins and with their limbs removed, they were sometimes thought to live perpetually airborne in the highest parts of the sky.about worth of it Here, the Amerindians.note King Hieron … than Simonides did by his The poet Simonides of Ceos spent his final years at the court of Hieron I of Syracuse – see above, – where he is said to have helped reconcile Hieron with the tyrant Theron of Acragas (Agrigento).note that Encyclopaedian, all the learning in the world The word ‘encyclopaedian’ here is used as a noun, its unusual form deriving from the retention of the Greek accusative ending. It refers to the ideal of ‘general’ or polymathic knowledge that was especially prized in Oxford at the time (see the editor’s Introduction).about Poetical divinity Creative or artistic accounts of the gods – that is, in classical mythology.about Helicon A classical mythological allusion to poetic inspiration. The Boeotian mountain, described by Hesiod as his own inspiration in the opening of the Theogony, was sacred to the Muses as the location of the Aganippe and Hippocrene springs, the drinking of whose waters was said to induce poetic ecstasy.about Errant motions Roving or wandering movements (of the planets, by contrast with the fixed positions of the stars).note those all-devouring municipal Laws The complaint here refers to the domination of the ‘municipal laws’ (the laws of particular states, and so here, English common law) over the ‘civil law’ (the legal system historically derived from Roman law) that prevailed in continental Europe and was studied by learned ‘civilian’ lawyers. In Burton’s time, the number of doctors of civil law graduating from the English universities had declined significantly, after their profession suffered a series of attacks by common lawyers, and the jurisdiction of civil law became diminished by prohibitions issued by superior common law courts preventing them from proceeding with suits. After 1625, however, the role of civil law in ecclesiastical and admiralty courts was restrengthened by Charles I and Archbishop William Laud.see Quacksalvers, Paracelsians See above, and .gloss cast Dismissed, sacked.gloss Goodwives The mistress of a household.gloss a brief An abstract or summary.source as it was not many years … this land John Howson (1556/7–1632), one of Burton’s colleagues at Christ Church, became bishop of Oxford in 1619, and subsequently, in 1628, bishop of Durham. The sermon quoted here, on Matthew 21:12–13, was actually delivered on 4 December 1597; for ‘Paul’s cross’, see above, .note as Phalaris objected to the Leontines … fear In the letter quoted here, purporting to be from the Sicilian tyrant Phalaris – see above, – to the Spartan king Leonidas I (reigned c. 490–480 BCE) in the midst of a conflict over the colony of Leontini, Phalaris claims that a captured spy has told him that Leonidas is destitute of everything except fear and hunger. The ‘Epistles of Phalaris’ were later proved to be spurious, and probably originating in the second century CE.note for the lease of a life That is, for a lease which remains in force until the death of the person to which it was granted.note copyhold An ancient form of customary tenure, by which lands were held as a portion of a manor, at the will of the landowner and certified only by the transcript (or ‘copy’) of a manorial court record.source thunder-clap A quotation from Ulrich von Hutten’s dialogue Aula sive Misaulus (1518), where the subject is actually the daily routine of the courtier.note Thalia The sense of the partial Latin quotation in note ‘e’, which is adapted from the Anacreontica (1554) by Julius Caesar Scaliger, is clarified by the original: ‘Si furor est Cupido,/Si furor est Lyaeus, Si furor est Thalia,/Quoties furor, furor, furor/Amans, bibens, poeta?’ (‘If madness is Cupid,/If madness is Bacchus,/If madness is Thalia,/How often do I become mad, mad, mad/In loving, drinking, {being} a poet?’) ‘Thalia’ is the Muse of comedy and idyllic poetry.source millers’ coats Evidently a loose allusion to the account of Cleanthes given by Diogenes Laertius – see above, – who also reports that the philosopher wore no shirt under his cloak (7.5.169).gloss except Object, protest.gloss scamble In note ‘f’, struggle or scramble.source non pranderet olus A reference to a phrase in Horace (Epistles 1.17.13), which itself alludes to a story reported by Diogenes Laertius (2.8.68). When the philosopher Aristippus – on whom, see above, – walked by Diogenes the Cynic, who was cleaning vegetables, the latter said to him, ‘If you had learned to make these your diet, you would not have paid court to kings.’ Aristippus replied, ‘And if you knew how to associate with men, you would not be washing vegetables.’gloss baffled Disgraced, treated with contempt.about rich Crassus An allusion to the Roman general and politician Marcus Licinius Crassus (115–53 BCE), the triumvir whose great wealth was famous in the late Roman Republic, and would subsequently become proverbial.about offered unto him The Greek rhetorician Libanius of Antioch (314–c. 393 CE) is reported by Eunapius, perhaps unreliably, to have refused the honorary title of praetorian prefect when it was offered by unnamed emperors who ruled after Julian, with the comment that the title of sophist was ‘more distinguished’ (Lives of the Philosophers and Sophists 496).source Achan-like Achan was stoned and burned for stealing some of the spoils of Jericho, which had been consecrated for the treasury of the Lord’s House; this resulted in the collective punishment of the Israelites by God (Joshua 7:1–26). His name is hence associated with greed or simony.gloss embezzled Squandered.gloss moil Work hard, drudge.gloss lighten Flash lightning.source as the enchanted Adder … ears In Psalm 58:4–5, the poison of the wicked is compared to that of a serpent: ‘they are like the deaf adder that stoppeth her ear; which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely.’note the Bawd in Plautus Ballio, the pimp in Pseudolus – see above, 1.2.3.6, p. 261.source that Miser … in arca The rich Athenian miser described by Horace in Satires 1.1.about Simoniacal contractors Greedy traders in ecclesiastical property.note foul ends ‘He’ may be the Oxford clergyman and Fellow of Oriel College John Day, in a sermon printed in Day’s Festivals (1615), although William Camden also recorded the proverb in his Remains (1614).source as an Eagle’s feathers … substance According to Pliny the Elder (10.4), the feathers of the eagle, if mixed with those of other birds, will destroy them.note aurum Tholosanum That is, stolen and cursed gold. ‘Toulousain gold’ refers to the treasure of the Tectosages, allegedly plundered from the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi by Gallic invaders in 279 BCE, and taken from Toulouse by the Roman general Quintus Servilius Caepio in 106 BCE. Caepio was disgraced and his family impoverished, and the belief subsequently circulated that touching the gold brought misfortune.note all together The fable of ‘The Eagle and the Fox’.gloss Church-chopping Dealing in ecclesiastical benefices.gloss painful Diligent, painstaking.gloss Sciences Branches of learning.note nescit vivere The Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund – see above, – had this saying, according to Enea Silvio Piccolomini (Pope Pius II).gloss trivantly A lazy person; or, more strongly, an idle rogue.about Polyanthean helps A polyanthea is an anthology or commonplace book, collecting excerpts or quotations from literature.note pen and Ink-horn men Bookish men; the ink-horn was a small container, originally made of a horn, for holding writing ink.note humane learning Writers on divinity and the ‘humanities’ – the classically orientated studia humanitatis of poetry, rhetoric, grammar, history and moral philosophy.about Land-leapers Or ‘land-lopers’: literally, ‘vagabonds’; but here, figuratively, ‘adventurers’ or ‘explorers’.about Julian In this list of learned Roman emperors, ‘Antoninus’ is probably Marcus Aurelius (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus) rather than Antoninus Pius, and ‘Severus’ is Septimius Severus; the ostensibly odd inclusion of Nero perhaps relates to his love of poetry and music, or to his relationship with Seneca.about Michael the Emperor, and Isacius Two medieval emperors of Byzantium, Michael VII Doukas – on whom, see above, – and Isaac I Komnenos, who ruled 1057–9.about Orion, Perseus, Alphonsus, Ptolemaeus, famous Astronomers This list begins peculiarly with two Greek heroes with constellations named after them, before introducing the astronomer Claudius Ptolemaeus (Ptolemy) – included, perhaps, because of his occasional (erroneous) association with the Egyptian dynasty of the Ptolemies – and Alfonso X, ‘the Wise’ (1221–84), king of Castile, León and Galicia, who sponsored the creation of the ‘Alfonsine Tables’ of astronomical data, which were influential across Europe until the seventeenth century.about Sapor, Mithridates, Lysimachus, admired Physicians On Sapor – included here because he was credited with the invention of various medicinal syrups, including ‘King Sabor’s Syrup’ for melancholy – see above, and 2.4.1.5, p. 633; on Mithridates, see above, ; King Lysimachus (360–281 BCE) who ruled Thrace, Asia Minor and Macedon is apparently confused here with the Hippocratic physician Lysimachus of Cos (fl. c. 100 BCE).note Evax that Arabian prince … an exquisite Philosopher Some manuscripts and early printed editions of Pliny the Elder’s Natural History contain a passage describing the Arabian king Evax as having dedicated a book on the subject of medical herbs to the emperor Nero. Burton made this reference in his first edition of 1621, but in 1629 the passage in Pliny was shown by the French scholar Claude Saumaise to have been a medieval interpolation. Evax was also spuriously reported to have written a work on the properties of precious stones.about Anacreon to Polycrates The Greek lyric poet Anacreon (582–485 BCE) enjoyed the patronage of Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos, for whom he was said to have composed laudatory odes.source Xenocrates According to Diogenes Laertius (4.2), the philosopher Xenocrates (b. 396/5 BCE) served as head of the Platonic Academy in Athens for twenty-five years, until his death at the age of eighty-two.gloss Clerks Scholars.note velut in Lycaeum … University The Latin word ‘Lyceum’ derives from the name of the ancient Athenian gymnasium dedicated to Apollo Lyceus, which hosted the school of Aristotle, and later became the generic term for a university (or other educational institution).source Archelaus … suavi sermone According to Plutarch (Sayings of Kings and Commanders 177A), the Macedonian king Archelaus (413–399 BCE), on being asked by one of his guests at dinner for a golden cup, ordered it to be given instead to Euripides, saying to the guest, ‘You are just the man to ask and not receive; he to receive even when he does not ask.’gloss chuff A coarse, rude person; or a greedy miser.gloss depression Lowered, or kept down.about Bavius and Mevius Two incompetent Roman poets satirized by Virgil and Horace.gloss elogies Eulogies.source Hieron The less well-known names in this list include Demaratus, a prominent Corinthian citizen of the fourth century BCE who, according to Plutarch (Alexander 9.12), helped to reconcile Philip of Macedon with his son Alexander after a domestic quarrel; the Thracian philosopher Anaxarchus (c. 380–c. 320 BCE), who obviously cannot have been a companion of Augustus, but who did accompany Alexander the Great on his Asian campaigns; and the Roman jurists Gaius Trebatius Testa (c. 84 BCE–c. 4 CE) and Gaius Cassius Longinus, who lived in the mid-first century CE. For Simonides and Hieron, see above, and .note as Paterculus of Cato Cato the Younger – see above, .note amongst us A reference, added in the third edition (1628), to Charles I, who ascended the English throne at the death of his father James I on 27 March 1625. The effect of this passage on readers would have changed dramatically in the sixth edition (1651), issued after Burton’s own death but also after the execution of Charles in 1649.note Sir Huon of Bordeaux, Amadis de Gaul Late medieval French and Spanish chivalric romances, popular among the gentry and nobility in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and parodied in Don Quixote.gloss Outlandish Foreign.gloss submissness Humility, submissiveness.gloss censure Judgement, opinion.gloss ingeniously Ingenuously, honestly.gloss deboshed Debauched.note stocks In the light of the Latin phrase immediately following, probably livestock; alternatively, blocks of wood or tree-stumps, figuratively denoting insensible or stupid people; or just ‘lines of descent’ or family (that is, ‘mere titles’).note barbarous Thracians Thracians were commonly regarded by ancient Greeks and Romans as bloodthirsty barbarians.source brick An allusion to Exodus 5:6–21, where the enslaved Israelites are commanded by Pharaoh to manufacture their full quota of bricks without their usual supply of straw.note no penny, no Paternoster That is, the priest will not perform without prior payment.gloss feed, and made Paid a fee, and have their well-being assured.source ut Cerberus offa … to hell A reference to Virgil (Aeneid 6.417–21), where Cerberus, the dog who guards the entrance to the underworld, is lured by the Cumaean Sibyl into eating a morsel of food covered in honey and imbued with a soporific drug (the Latin phrase means ‘as Cerberus was by a morsel’) – thereby helping Aeneas on his journey.source Omnia Romae venalia The saying derives from the condemnation of ancient Rome expressed by the Numidian king Jugurtha (c. 160–104 BCE) in Sallust’s War with Jugurtha (20.1).gloss extraordinary parts Good qualities.gloss indurate Stubborn.gloss entertainment Paid employment or service.source he shall serve … Jacob did for Rachel In Genesis 29:16–30, Jacob agrees to work for Rachel’s uncle Laban for seven years in order to marry her; after Laban tricks him into marrying Rachel’s sister Leah, Jacob has to work for another seven years for the hand of his beloved.gloss come off soundly Hand over a large amount of money.note precise Both ‘nice’ and ‘curious’ here mean ‘fastidious’, or ‘exceedingly careful and precise’ – qualities often derogatorily attributed to contemporary puritans, who are also the ‘schismatics’ being accused here of destroying the unity of the English Church.gloss serve the turn Satisfy requirements.note hidebound Calves in a Pasture Calves whose skin clings tightly to the back and ribs, as a consequence of malnutrition and emaciation.gloss arrearages Debts, arrears.note first fruits … procurations All types of monetary levy payable to the Crown or the Church.about Beginae Beguine sisters – members of lay sisterhoods, founded in the twelfth century and mainly located in the Low Countries.gloss Sectaries (Religious) schismatics.source those wild beasts of Ephesus A borrowing from 1 Corinthians 15:32: ‘If after the manner of men I have fought with beasts at Ephesus’ – Paul was probably referring to the devotees of Artemis in Ephesus – ‘what advantageth it me, if the dead rise not?’gloss terse Refined, cultured.gloss Graziers People who graze or feed cattle for the market.gloss Chapmen Merchants or traders.about Pontus Here, the Black Sea, where Ovid was banished by the emperor Augustus in 8 CE, to the town of Tomis (modern Constanta, in Romania).gloss Idiots Unskilled or untrained people.about Boor An unrefined rustic or peasant. The quotation is from Christopher Marlowe’s Hero and Leander (1598), where the punitive association of Mercury with Poverty, in a fable apparently invented by Marlowe, is ordained by the classical Fates.gloss litigious Quarrelsome, contentious (not necessarily in the legal sense).source Flacce Marones This quotation from Martial (Epigrams 8.55.5) alludes to the poets Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus) and Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).
